sense: through the air, over water, or over ice

terms.gloss: glide: move smoothly along, through the air, over water, or over ice
evidence: Verg. A. 6.202: liquidumque per āëra lāpsae (Lewis & Short, “of flying”)
Verg. A. 8.91: lābitur ūncta vadīs abiēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical verb for gliding, said of snakes, of ships, and of birds on the wing (Lewis & Short); Traupman uses it of skating on rollerblades. Of a child standing on a balance bike, stāns lābitur. Losing one’s footing is the same verb in another of its senses (see slip).

phrases.english: and gliding through the clear air (of doves)
gliding on wings through the air
the tarred fir glides over the shallows (of a ship)
The children are gliding over the ice.

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
